overview: Friday's news is dominated by Cyclone Akvan hitting the Odisha coast, the aftermath of a Trump-Xi-Putin summit in China, and a sharp sell-off in AI stocks after Anthropic's record IPO, while the rupee firmed and gold fell.

market_snapshot.label: Gold
market_snapshot.value: lowest level of 2026 in one report

items.headline: Cyclone Akvan makes landfall on the Odisha coast
items.summary: Cyclone Akvan has begun its landfall in Odisha, bringing rough seas and strong winds to the coastal districts, after days of evacuation warnings.
items.detail: Live reports say the coastal districts of Odisha are seeing rough sea conditions and strong winds as landfall begins. Other reports say the storm weakened before reaching land, but still brought heavy rain to Odisha, Andhra Pradesh and parts of West Bengal. In Andhra Pradesh's Srikakulam district, low-lying areas in Ichchapuram and Sompeta were reported flooded. The India Meteorological Department has issued a rain alert for south Bengal running until Saturday.
items.analysis: Cyclone risk along this coast is a recurring concern, and the pace at which the storm weakens in the coming hours will decide how much damage the flooding causes.

items.headline: US, China and Russia leaders hold a historic summit in Shenzhen
items.summary: Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin met in a trilateral summit in China, a format rarely seen, and commentators are divided on how much it achieved.
items.detail: The Hindu reported the summit as a historic gathering of the US, China and Russia. The Indian Express and The Conversation described it as heavy on symbolism and light on substance, with the three leaders discussing nuclear weapons but not much else. Financial Times coverage framed it as a Chinese moment that some in Beijing compared to Yalta, while The Guardian called it more of a footnote. The Washington Post said Xi put himself and China at the centre of the meeting.
items.analysis: Views differ sharply on whether the meeting signals a real shift in great-power politics or mainly staged a show of unity, so the follow-up statements will matter more than the photographs.

items.headline: Anthropic's record IPO fails to lift the AI sector as markets sell off
items.summary: Anthropic's IPO raised a record sum and its shares rose on debut, but a wider AI-led sell-off has since hit Asian and global markets.
items.detail: Reports say Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in the biggest IPO on record and its shares closed 17 percent higher on the first day of trading. Reuters' Morning Bid column said the splashy listing had failed to lift the AI sector, and Asian shares were heading for their worst week since 2020. Nasdaq was reported to have fallen 2.3 percent in one session, pulling down Asian markets. Indian indices opened lower as technology and metal stocks weighed.
items.analysis: The episode tests how far investor enthusiasm for AI can carry valuations, and it shows how quickly a sell-off in one sector can spread to markets far away.

items.headline: UN top court finds Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya
items.summary: The International Court of Justice ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, a landmark judgment in international law.
items.detail: The ICJ found Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya Muslim minority. The BBC's Jeremy Bowen called the verdict historic and said it could have far-reaching implications. Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh welcomed the ruling but said they want to return home to Myanmar. Chinese state-aligned commentary has defended Myanmar's position, reflecting the divided diplomatic response. The Conversation argued the ruling may affect other cases, including cases involving Israel.
items.analysis: The verdict's practical effect on Myanmar and on the refugees depends on enforcement, which the court cannot carry out on its own, so attention will turn to diplomatic and legal follow-up.

items.headline: Britain and the EU move towards a relations reset, but divisions remain
items.summary: The UK and the EU are close to agreeing steps to reset their post-Brexit relationship, including a possible youth mobility scheme, though differences persist.
items.detail: Reuters reports that Britain and the EU are set to agree a reset, but divisions persist. The BBC understands the two sides will agree a youth mobility scheme, which would let young people from each side live and work in the other for a period. Al Jazeera describes the deal as steps towards a reset rather than a full agreement. CNN's coverage this week asked whether the UK is preparing to undo Brexit, a question that remains politically sensitive in both London and Brussels.
items.analysis: The reset is incremental, so the key test will be whether the agreed steps on mobility and trade are carried through and whether they hold up domestically.

items.headline: White House fires its cybersecurity chief after widespread tech outages
items.summary: The Trump administration has removed the national cyber director after a wave of technology outages hit the United States.
items.detail: Reports say Sean Cairncross was fired after widespread outages affected the US. Trump has backed the decision, and Axios reported that Kirsten Davies is to be named the new national cyber director. The Guardian described the outages as a wave of tech failures that hit the country. The national cyber director coordinates federal cybersecurity policy, so the change of leadership comes at a sensitive time for government digital systems.
items.analysis: Replacing the official responsible for cyber policy after a visible failure raises questions about how the government will handle security and resilience going forward.

items.headline: US Senate passes sweeping energy permitting reform in 62-33 vote
items.summary: The Senate has passed a major permitting reform bill on energy projects, backed by parts of the energy and AI sectors but criticised by environmental groups.
items.detail: The Senate passed the energy permitting reform bill by 62 votes to 33. CNBC reported that the bill is backed by AI and energy industries. The Center for Biological Diversity criticised Senate Democrats for advancing the bill, arguing it would bring environmental harm, while The Breakthrough Institute welcomed the passage. Permitting reform aims to speed up approvals for power lines, pipelines and other infrastructure, which the bill's supporters say is needed for growing power demand.
items.analysis: The vote suggests a rare bipartisan majority on speeding up infrastructure, but the environmental trade-offs will shape how the bill is implemented.

items.headline: Europe weighs the cost of Ukraine's defence as Trump-Putin talks stall
items.summary: European leaders are counting the cost of supporting Ukraine and say they are ready for talks with Russia, even as a direct Trump-Putin meeting has not delivered a settlement.
items.detail: Al Jazeera reports that Europe is counting the cost of Ukraine's defence, far from the Trump-Putin meeting. The BBC reported that European leaders say they are ready for talks with Russia on ending the war. A Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin brought together Ukraine's allies, but The Guardian reported that some warned a 'Yalta format' would not bring peace. European leaders are weighing how to fund support for Ukraine while also seeking a route to negotiations.
items.analysis: Europe's role in any peace process has been questioned, so the balance between funding Ukraine and opening channels to Moscow is a central question to watch.

items.headline: Rahul Gandhi says India is a side player in geopolitics and attacks the PM over the summit
items.summary: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi has shared a picture of the G3 leaders and said a compromised prime minister cannot sit at that table, prompting a BJP response.
items.detail: Rahul Gandhi shared a picture of the US, China and Russia leaders and said India is a side player in geopolitics. He said a compromised PM can never sit at that table, a reference to Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The BJP responded with a jibe calling Congress 'Pak fanboys', according to NDTV's report. The exchange comes after an earlier row this week over Rahul Gandhi's remarks in the US on Indian democracy, which the BJP said went against the country's democratic fabric.
items.analysis: The BJP and Congress view India's foreign policy very differently, so the debate reflects a broader argument about the government's approach to the world's major powers.

items.headline: Women's reservation constitutional amendment fails in the Lok Sabha
items.summary: A constitutional amendment bill on women's reservation in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies failed to pass in the lower house of Parliament.
items.detail: News On AIR reported that the constitutional amendment bill on women's reservation in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies failed in the Lok Sabha. A constitutional amendment needs a two-thirds majority of members present and voting, so failure in the house is a major political setback for the bill's supporters. Separately, Parliament is considering a Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (Amendment) Bill, 2026 and a jobs quota for less well-off people not covered by affirmative action, according to parliamentary records.
items.analysis: The result will shape how parties position themselves on women's representation ahead of future sessions, and the reasons for the failure will be scrutinised.

items.headline: Election Commission says its SIR decisions were unanimous, as opposition and courts scrutinise voter-roll work
items.summary: The Election Commission says all decisions, including on the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls, were taken unanimously, while the opposition questions the process.
items.detail: The Election Commission of India said all its decisions, including those on the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter rolls, were taken unanimously by the full Commission. The Reporters' Collective reported that in Delhi the ECI bent its own rules to bring back deleted voters, a claim the Commission has not accepted in these reports. The Supreme Court directed the ECI to verify alleged fraudulent Form 7 deletions in Delhi. The Supreme Court also declined urgent listing of a plea seeking recall of a split verdict on the law governing EC appointments.
items.analysis: Voter-roll revision is a sensitive area, and the court-directed verification will be important for public confidence in the accuracy of electoral lists.

items.headline: Justice Yashwant Varma tells Parliament his resignation is not an admission of wrongdoing
items.summary: Justice Yashwant Varma has told Parliament that his resignation does not mean he admits wrongdoing, saying he is innocent in the cash-at-home row.
items.detail: Justice Yashwant Varma said in a letter or statement to Parliament that his resignation is not an admission of wrongdoing and that he is innocent. The matter relates to a cash-at-home row that has been under scrutiny. Under the Indian process for judges, Parliament can take up complaints about a sitting judge, and the resignation changes the procedural path of that inquiry. Both his own position and the wider questions about accountability in the judiciary are being debated.
items.analysis: The case is a test of how judicial accountability works when a judge resigns before any finding, and the outcome will be watched closely by the legal community.

items.headline: Enforcement Directorate raids across Kerala in gold smuggling and hawala probe
items.summary: The Enforcement Directorate has searched multiple locations across Kerala in connection with suspected gold smuggling and hawala transactions, and a separate FEMA probe is also under way.
items.detail: Several reports say the Enforcement Directorate conducted simultaneous searches across Keralam in a suspected gold smuggling and hawala probe. The Hindu separately reported ED searches as part of a probe into alleged Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA) violations. The ED is a central agency that investigates money laundering and foreign exchange offences, and its searches usually involve seizing documents and digital records. No charges were detailed in these headlines, and the investigations are at an early stage.
items.analysis: Searches are investigative steps rather than verdicts, so the next signals will come from any formal charges or statements from the agency.

items.headline: Kerala weighs restoring staff benefits, including leave surrender, pay revision and MEDISEP
items.summary: The Kerala government is considering bringing back several employee benefits, including leave surrender, pay revision and the MEDISEP health scheme.
items.detail: Livemint reports that Kerala is considering restoration of several benefits for government staff. The list includes leave surrender, pay revision and MEDISEP, a state health insurance scheme for government employees and pensioners. Such benefits are often pared back during fiscal stress and restored later as finances improve. The reports do not give final decisions or costs, so the proposal is at the consideration stage.
items.analysis: Restoring benefits would affect the state budget and public-sector morale, so the final decisions and their fiscal cost will be the key details to watch.

items.headline: Kerala Home Minister seeks review of juvenile justice age limit amid crime concerns
items.summary: Kerala's Home Minister has asked for a review of the age limit in the juvenile justice law, citing growing concern about crime.
items.detail: The South First reports that the Keralam Home Minister has sought a review of the age limit under the juvenile justice law amid growing crime concerns. The juvenile justice system in India treats children in conflict with the law differently from adults, and the age cut-off decides which cases fall under that system. Changing the age limit is a national matter under central law, so any state push would need to go through the central framework. Public debate on whether the current limit is right is likely to continue.
items.analysis: The debate pits concern about serious crime against the principle of treating children differently, and the answer will depend on the evidence presented to lawmakers.

items.headline: Great Nicobar port could erase Galathea Bay's leatherback turtle population
items.summary: A report warns that the planned port at Great Nicobar could wipe out the leatherback turtles nesting at Galathea Bay and their unique genetic diversity.
items.detail: Scroll.in reports that last winter female leatherback turtles came ashore on a beach bordering Galathea Bay on Great Nicobar Island to lay eggs in 869 nests. The article argues that the planned port could erase this nesting population and its unique genetic diversity. The Great Nicobar project, which includes a port and township, has been contested over concerns for forests, wildlife and the rights of tribal communities. A separate report this week said Rs 5 crore was approved for an optical fibre link to Galathea Bay.
items.analysis: The project's environmental costs remain the central point of dispute, and the turtle nesting data is likely to feature in future clearance debates.

items.headline: COP31 climate draft drops fossil fuels as talks enter the final day
items.summary: The latest COP31 draft climate deal no longer mentions fossil fuels, as talks in Antalya enter their final day amid deep divisions.
items.detail: ThePrint reports that fossil fuels have vanished from the latest COP31 climate deal draft. The Guardian's live coverage says the talks are at a crunch point and deeply divided as they enter the final day. The Mongabay India report notes that the draft on electrification may be weaker than an ambitious goal to raise electricity's share of final energy use to 35 percent by 2035. India has pressed for accountability on climate finance and a fair global stocktake at the summit.
items.analysis: Whether fossil fuels remain in the final text will be a key signal of how much ambition the summit can agree on, and India's stance on finance will matter to the outcome.

items.headline: India's weak monsoon and El Nino raise concerns about water and farming
items.summary: A weak monsoon and the approaching El Nino phase are raising concerns about water supply and industry, and an Indian ocean agency has put the odds of El Nino high.
items.detail: Nikkei Asia reports that India's weak monsoon and El Nino are highlighting water problems for industry. Mongabay India reports that the Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services has confirmed an 80 to 100 percent probability of a persistent El Nino phase, and warns this could deepen water stress in Tamil Nadu and threaten agriculture. El Nino is a natural warming of the Pacific that often weakens the Indian monsoon, and climate change is increasing the impact of such cycles.
items.analysis: El Nino is a natural cycle, but a warmer climate can make its effects on rainfall and water stress more severe, so planning for water use is becoming more urgent.

items.headline: Bupa launches a hybrid PMI and IPMI plan for UK residents with European cover
items.summary: Bupa has launched a hybrid private medical insurance plan for UK residents that includes access to treatment across Europe.
items.detail: ITIJ and Health and Protection report that Bupa has launched a private medical insurance plan for UK residents, called Bupa By You Sapphire. The plan combines domestic private medical insurance with international cover and adds benefits such as fertility, maternity and chronic condition care. It also gives access to treatment in 30 European Economic Area countries. The product sits in the growing category of hybrid plans that blend domestic and international protection.
items.analysis: Hybrid plans like this show insurers responding to customers who live and move across borders, a trend that also matters for expatriate health cover.

items.headline: IRDAI moves to add real-time tracking of health insurance claims
items.summary: India's insurance regulator is planning live tracking of mediclaims and has formed working groups to improve transparency on health claims.
items.detail: Telegraph India and India Business Trade report that the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) plans live tracking for mediclaims to improve transparency. Asia Insurance Post reports that the chairman has said two working groups will be formed to look at health claims transparency. Policyholders often struggle to see where a claim stands, and the regulator's plan aims to address that gap. The details of timelines and rules are not yet clear from these reports.
items.analysis: Real-time visibility could reduce disputes over claims, but the rules on what data is shared and how quickly will decide whether the change is useful in practice.

items.headline: IRDAI chief warns about consumer data collection before insurance price quotes
items.summary: The IRDAI chairman has flagged the risk of insurers collecting consumer data before providing price quotes, along with broader AI-related risks.
items.detail: MediaNama and Business Standard report that the IRDAI chairman flagged a consumer data grab before insurance price quotes, as well as AI-related risks. The Times of India reported separately that the regulator has flagged conflicts of interest where banks and auto companies sell insurance. These concerns relate to fair pricing and whether customers understand what they are sharing. The regulator's position is a warning rather than a new rule in these reports.
items.analysis: Data use and conflicts of interest in distribution are likely to shape future rules, so insurers may need to explain their pricing practices more clearly.

items.headline: Dubai International Airport resumes flights after a drone strike on a fuel tank
items.summary: Dubai International Airport has resumed flights after a drone strike hit a fuel tank, as regional airspace warnings remain in place.
items.detail: News On AIR reports that Dubai International Airport has resumed flights after a drone strike on a fuel tank. Gulf News has published flight status updates with cancellations, delays and travel alerts for the day. Airlines including Etihad, flydubai and Lufthansa Group have extended suspensions on some routes, while Qatar Airways has resumed flights to Riyadh and Dammam. EASA has extended its Middle East conflict bulletins to 31 January 2027.
items.analysis: Travellers should check their airline before flying, since the disruptions are changing quickly and may last into next year.

items.headline: Somalia expels the UAE ambassador, accusing Abu Dhabi of violating its sovereignty
items.summary: Somalia has ordered the UAE ambassador to leave the country, accusing Abu Dhabi of an invasion and violation of sovereignty.
items.detail: Al Jazeera and Reuters report that Somalia has expelled the UAE ambassador, citing an invasion and accusing Abu Dhabi of violating its sovereignty. The reports do not give the UAE's detailed response in these headlines. Diplomatic expulsions are a serious step short of a formal break in relations, and they often reflect long-running disputes over security or influence in the Horn of Africa. Relations between the two countries will now depend on whether talks follow.
items.analysis: The move is significant for Gulf diplomacy in the Horn of Africa, and what Abu Dhabi says next will indicate whether the dispute is likely to escalate.

items.headline: Emiratisation in Dubai's private sector up 350 percent over four years, says Sheikh Hamdan
items.summary: Dubai's Crown Prince Sheikh Hamdan has said Emirati employment in the private sector has risen by 350 percent over four years.
items.detail: Dubai Eye 103.8 reports that Sheikh Hamdan said Emiratisation in Dubai's private sector has risen 350 percent over four years. Emiratisation refers to the UAE's policy of increasing the share of Emirati citizens in private-sector jobs, which has quotas and targets for companies. The headline gives the growth rate but not the starting figure, so the percentage should be read as growth from a base rather than an absolute share. The UAE has set this policy as part of its long-term workforce plans.
items.analysis: The headline growth rate is large, but its meaning depends on the starting point, so the absolute number of Emirati workers will be the more useful measure.

items.headline: Saudi Arabia overtakes the UAE as India's second-largest oil supplier
items.summary: Saudi Arabia has moved ahead of the UAE to become India's No. 2 oil supplier, while Russia remains the top source.
items.detail: ET EnergyWorld reports that Saudi Arabia has overtaken the UAE as India's No. 2 oil supplier, with Russia keeping the lead. The shift comes amid regional conflict that has affected shipping and energy flows across the Gulf. Iran's recent tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, reported by Insurance Journal, have added to security concerns. Saudi Arabia also confirmed a strike on its PIF tower after Houthi attacks, as reported by The National.
items.analysis: Shifts in supplier rankings reflect both price and security, so the trend will be watched by Indian refiners and by anyone tracking Gulf energy risk.

items.headline: Indian markets open lower as the global AI sell-off weighs on sentiment
items.summary: Sensex and Nifty opened lower on Friday as a sell-off in global technology stocks and a weak Wall Street session weighed on sentiment.
items.detail: Several reports from Friday morning say the Sensex and Nifty opened lower as weakness in global technology stocks spread. Telangana Today reported the Sensex losing 615 points in early trade, though Fortune India later reported the Sensex rebounding about 1,400 points from the day's low. The GIFT Nifty signalled a gap-down open after falling more than 200 points, following a Nasdaq drop of 2.3 percent. Profit-taking after a recent rally and cautious global cues were also cited as reasons for the weakness.
items.analysis: The large intraday swings show nervousness in the market, and the closing levels will show whether the rebound in later trade held.

items.headline: Rupee rises past 93 per dollar to a seven-month high on foreign inflows
items.summary: The rupee gained to 93.15 against the dollar, hitting a seven-month high as foreign investors bought Indian equities and oil prices eased.
items.detail: The Hindu reported the rupee strengthening 17 paise to 93.15 against the US dollar. Business Standard said it had risen past 93 for the first time since April, helped by foreign portfolio inflows and softer oil. Reuters reported that the rupee had risen past 93 as the AI rout drew billions into India while speculators bailed out of positions. Jefferies' Chris Wood has also said he is increasing exposure to Indian equities while cutting Taiwan, as AI stocks fall.
items.analysis: A stronger rupee helps importers and eases inflation pressure, but it can also be a sign that money is flowing in as investors move away from AI-heavy markets.

items.headline: Gold heads for its worst week in months as Fed rate-hike bets grow
items.summary: Gold and silver prices have fallen sharply this week on a stronger dollar and rising expectations of US interest-rate hikes.
items.detail: Kotak Neo reports that gold prices have plunged more than 7 percent this week and are heading for their worst fall since March. CNBC said gold was set for its worst week in eight months as a firm dollar and Fed hike bets weighed on prices. Gold and silver ETFs have also dropped, according to TradingView and Business Standard. J.P. Morgan has said it expects Fed rate hikes at each of the next three meetings as inflation persists, while the Fed has signalled lower pay increases for regional staff in 2027.
items.analysis: Gold tends to move against higher interest rates and a stronger dollar, so the next US inflation data and Fed signals will largely set its direction.

items.headline: Asian shares head for their worst week since 2020 as AI valuations come under pressure
items.summary: Asian share markets are on course for their worst week since 2020 as concerns about AI valuations and the prospect of higher US rates weigh on global equities.
items.detail: Reuters reports that Asian shares are heading for their worst week since 2020 as the AI rout deepens. The sell-off follows a Nasdaq drop reported at 2.3 percent, and Wall Street's weakness spread to Asian exchanges. Analysts quoted in these reports point to AI valuation concerns and hawkish Fed signals as drivers. Some investors have moved money into markets less exposed to chips, such as India, according to South China Morning Post coverage of the flow.
items.analysis: The sell-off shows how concentrated market gains in AI stocks have become, so a fall in that sector can drag down broader indices.

items.headline: Jensen Huang leaves Nvidia and the AI roadmap faces questions
items.summary: Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang will not return as CEO, prompting analysis of what his exit means for the chipmaker and the wider AI roadmap.
items.detail: The Hindu reports on how Jensen Huang's exit from Nvidia alters the AI roadmap. Reports say the Nvidia board has said he will not be reinstated as CEO. Rest of World reports the departure removes Beijing's biggest advocate in Silicon Valley, accelerates chip stockpiling and leaves Asian suppliers bracing for what comes next. Several industry leaders have commented publicly, including OpenAI's Sam Altman, who said it is hard to imagine the AI industry without Jensen.
items.analysis: Leadership changes at the company that makes most of the world's AI chips can ripple through supply chains and the policy debate over exports to China.

items.headline: Google DeepMind releases Gemini 4 Neon, a frontier coding agent
items.summary: Google DeepMind has introduced Gemini 4 Neon, which it describes as a frontier coding agent, and it is being added to GitHub Copilot.
items.detail: AI Magazine reports that Google DeepMind has launched Gemini 4 Neon as a frontier coding agent. Google's blog describes it as a new release, and The GitHub Blog reports that Gemini 4 Neon is being added to GitHub Copilot. A separate Google release, Gemini 4 Hydrogen, is aimed at a faster model for general-purpose robotics. Coding agents are AI systems that can write, test and fix software with limited human input.
items.analysis: Coding agents are becoming a major battleground between AI companies, and their real-world reliability will matter more than launch claims.

items.headline: Google builds a closed 'Mirror Dimension' web to test Chrome AI agents
items.summary: Google has built a large simulated internet, called Mirror Dimension, to test browser-based AI agents safely.
items.detail: WIRED reports that Google built a giant mirror internet to test its Chrome AI agents. Google's own blog describes Mirror Dimension as a way to evaluate browser-use agents without needing the live web. Moneycontrol describes it as a closed web environment for training agents. The approach allows the company to test how agents behave without risks to real websites or users.
items.analysis: Simulated test environments may become a standard way to check AI agents before they operate on the open web, which is a safety-relevant step.

items.headline: ISRO tests a semi-cryogenic engine power head at full thrust
items.summary: ISRO has tested the power head of its semi-cryogenic engine at full thrust, a step toward the engine's use in future launch vehicles.
items.detail: GK Today reports that ISRO has tested the semi-cryogenic engine power head at full thrust. Semi-cryogenic engines use kerosene and liquid oxygen, and they are seen as a cost-efficient option for future heavy-lift rockets. The test is one of a series of development steps for the engine. Separately, DD News reports that ISRO will soon fit one lakh fishing vessels with transponders it developed.
items.analysis: Full-thrust tests are a key milestone before an engine is used on a rocket, so the next test results will show how close the design is to flight use.

items.headline: China's longest hydrogen pipeline starts operations, fed by a green hydrogen plant
items.summary: China has begun operating its longest hydrogen pipeline, supplied by a 200 MW green hydrogen plant.
items.detail: Hydrogen Insight and Upstream Online report that China's longest hydrogen pipeline has started operations. The pipeline is supplied by a 200 megawatt green hydrogen plant, meaning hydrogen made by splitting water with renewable electricity. Pipelines can move hydrogen from production sites to industrial users far more cheaply than trucks at large volumes. Hydrogen transport and storage remain difficult challenges, and a related EU decision this week left hydrogen storage out of a grid permitting deal.
items.analysis: Operational hydrogen pipelines are rare, so performance data from this project will be closely watched by others planning similar networks.

items.headline: A lysine-derived carbon catalyst turns CO2 into cyclic carbonates without metals
items.summary: Researchers have shown a metal-free carbon catalyst, made from the amino acid lysine, that converts carbon dioxide into useful cyclic carbonates.
items.detail: Bioengineer.org reports a new study in which a carbon catalyst derived from lysine, an amino acid, converts carbon dioxide into cyclic carbonates. Cyclic carbonates are used in plastics, battery electrolytes and solvents, so turning CO2 into them is a route to using the gas rather than only storing it. Because the catalyst contains no metal, it avoids the cost and toxicity concerns of many catalysts. Related work this week also showed machine learning helping separate catalyst and reaction controls in CO2 conversion.
items.analysis: Metal-free catalysts are attractive for cost and sustainability, but the efficiency and scale of such processes will decide their practical value.

items.headline: arXiv paper: a graph neural network that predicts adsorption energies directly
items.summary: A new arXiv preprint describes AdsNet, a graph neural network that predicts how strongly molecules stick to surfaces, which is central to catalyst screening.
items.detail: In plain English, a new arXiv paper introduces AdsNet, a machine-learning model that predicts adsorption energy, which is how strongly a molecule binds to a catalyst surface. The authors say existing methods either run slowly, like full machine-learning potentials, or ignore geometry, which limits accuracy. AdsNet is designed to make a direct prediction and to remain sensitive to the local shape of the surface. Because adsorption energy is a key number in designing catalysts, faster accurate predictions could speed up screening of candidate materials.
items.analysis: Such models still need to be checked against experiments and density functional theory benchmarks before they can be trusted for new catalyst choices.

items.headline: arXiv paper: machine-learning screening of high-entropy carbides
items.summary: A new arXiv paper uses high-throughput machine-learning screening to search for promising high-entropy carbides, a family of ceramics with many metals mixed together.
items.detail: A new arXiv paper describes machine-learning screening of equimolar and non-equimolar high-entropy carbides. High-entropy carbides are ceramics that mix several metals in similar or unequal amounts, which creates a very large space of possible compositions. The authors say this space is too large to test by experiment or full ab initio calculations alone, so they screen it computationally. The approach aims to shortlist compositions worth making in the lab.
items.analysis: Screening tools like this are useful for narrowing huge search spaces, but the shortlisted materials still need synthesis and testing before any claims hold.

items.headline: Data centre air pollution can travel long distances, a study finds
items.summary: A study reports that air pollution from data centres can travel far beyond the sites themselves, widening the group of people exposed.
items.detail: Phys.org and Intelligent Living both report a study finding that data centre air pollution travels long distances. The coverage attributes the research to an MIT team, which examined how emissions from these facilities can be carried by winds. Data centres use large amounts of power, often from fossil-fuel grids and backup generators, so their emissions are a growing concern as AI demand rises. The findings suggest that siting decisions should consider wider air-quality effects than local impacts alone.
items.analysis: The study adds a new dimension to the debate about AI's energy footprint, pointing to health and planning issues that reach beyond the facility's fence line.

items.headline: The yttrium squeeze turns a little-known rare earth into a geopolitical lever
items.summary: A Lowy Institute analysis looks at how yttrium, a little-known rare earth, has become a point of pressure in China's supply chain policy.
items.detail: Lowy Institute's analysis describes yttrium as a little-known rare earth that has become China's latest geopolitical lever. Yttrium is used in products such as coatings, phosphors and some electronic and aerospace components. Rare earths are a sector in which China holds a large share of processing, so supply restrictions can have global effects. The piece is a reminder that critical materials beyond the more famous rare earths can carry significant strategic weight.
items.analysis: Supply pressure on a minor input can affect high-tech and defence manufacturing, so it is a useful signal of where trade tensions could next focus.
